Header: HER2 is a key therapeutic target in breast cancer, with its extracellular and intracellular domains driving tumor growth, survival, and resistance to treatment—particularly through the highly oncogenic, truncated p95HER2 form. Accurate assessment of HER2, including both full-length and truncated variants, is essential for guiding targeted therapies such as trastuzumab. Imaging mass cytometry, with its high dynamic range and multiplexing capability, enables precise, spatially resolved quantification of HER2 expression, offering a powerful tool for evaluating tumor heterogeneity and optimizing personalized treatment strategies.

Waypoints.Name: Tissue architecture
Waypoints.Description: Breast adenocarcinoma tissue architecture is shaped by the confined structure of the mammary ducts and interactions with the extracellular matrix, creating niches that influence tumor progression and metastasis. Markers such as pan-cytokeratin, CD45, CD31, and αSMA distinguish epithelial tumor cells, immune infiltrates, vasculature, and stromal components, respectively, aiding in the characterization of the tumor microenvironment.

Waypoints.Name: Myeloid cells
Waypoints.Description: Myeloid cells, including myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) and tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), drive breast adenocarcinoma progression by promoting immunosuppression, tumor invasion, and metastasis. Recruited by tumor-derived signals, these cells inhibit T-cell responses, support angiogenesis and stemness, and contribute to therapy resistance, making them key targets for strategies aimed at reshaping the tumor microenvironment.

Waypoints.Name: Lymphoid cells
Waypoints.Description: Lymphoid cells—comprising T cells, B cells, innate lymphoid cells, and natural killer (NK) cells—shape breast adenocarcinoma by mediating anti-tumor immunity through cytotoxic functions and tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (particularly CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ T cells) while also being subverted by the tumor microenvironment. Their dual roles in promoting and restraining tumor growth make lymphoid populations key targets for immunotherapeutic strategies.

Waypoints.Name: Immune activation
Waypoints.Description: Immune activation in breast adenocarcinoma is shaped by a complex interplay between tumor-promoting and immune-regulating factors within the tumor microenvironment, involving key molecules such as CD44, HLA-DR, CD7, CD38, and Granzyme B (GZMB). These biomarkers collectively influence tumor progression, immune evasion, and the effectiveness of anti-tumor immune responses by modulating processes like epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, antigen presentation, lymphocyte activation, and cytotoxicity.

Waypoints.Name: Tumor cell activation
Waypoints.Description: Tumor cell activation in breast adenocarcinoma is driven by biomarkers such as Ki-67, PD-L1, vimentin, and E-cadherin, which regulate proliferation, immune evasion, and metastatic potential. High Ki-67 and PD-L1 expression correlate with aggressive tumor behavior and poor prognosis, while increased vimentin and decreased E-cadherin mark epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, enhancing invasiveness and tumor progression.

Waypoints.Name: HER2 status
Waypoints.Description: HER2 is a crucial driver of breast adenocarcinoma progression, with its extracellular domain enabling ligand-independent dimerization and signaling, and its intracellular tyrosine kinase domain activating proliferative and survival pathways; the truncated p95HER2 form, lacking the extracellular domain, is significantly more oncogenic and contributes to therapeutic resistance. Imaging mass cytometry offers maximal dynamic range for evaluating HER2 expression, making it a powerful tool for distinguishing full-length versus truncated HER2 forms and accurately assessing HER2-driven tumor behavior and treatment response.
